newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. set to renew Iraqi "oil-for-food" deal.
newsitem.headline: U.N. set to renew Iraqi "oil-for-food" deal.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council was expected to approve late on Wednesday a six-month renewal of its "oil-for-food" deal with Iraq.
A resolution circulated among members will also say the council will consider favourably a further extension if it is satisfied Iraq ensures equitable distribution of humanitarian supplies.

Under the deal, which went into force on Dec. 10 and expires on June 7, Iraq has been allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy food, medicine and other necessities to help alleviate the effects of sanctions in force since its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The new council resolution would renew the arrangement for another 180-day period beginning at 12:01 a.m. EDT (0401 GMT) on June 8.

On the basis of reports from Secretary-General Kofi Annan and the U.N. sanctions committee, the council says it will conduct a "thorough review of all aspects" of the scheme after 90 days and again prior to the end of the 180-day period.

The resolution says the council "expresses its intention, prior to the end of the 180-day period, to consider favourably renewal of the provisions of this resolution, provided that the reports ... indicate that those provisions are being satisfactorily implemented."

A major preoccupation of the council has been to ensure that all sectors of the Iraqi population benefit from the supplies bought with the limited oil sales, not just those groups favoured by the Baghdad government. More than 100 U.N. observers have been deployed in the country to ensure this.

The resolution also directs the sanctions committee to "process expeditiously contract applications" submitted for the purchase of food and other supplies as soon as Annan has approved a new plan to be submitted by Iraq guaranteeing equitable distribution and describing items to be purchased.

Iraq has frequently complained that the sanctions committee, at the alleged instigation of the United States, has delayed approval of contracts for the purchase of humanitarian supplies. This led to a long delay before the goods began arriving in Iraq although arrangements for the sale of oil proceeded smoothly.

But a Clinton administration official said Washington was only following procedures that Iraq had demanded, such as Baghdad's signature on all goods contracts to make sure they were the proper ones. But he did say the United States had delayed non-food and medical contracts because the United Nations did not have enough monitors on the ground.

The official also said that the United States as well as Britain were unhappy with the lack of details in U.N. reports, prepared by the Department of Humanitarian Affairs, on how monitoring of the distribution of supplies was proceeding, particularly in the semi-autonomous Kurdish northern regions.

"We knew when the resolution was passed that this was going to be an area that was difficult," he said. "But we want to know from the (U.N.) secretariat what their teams are doing, how they are operating."
He said the U.N. was slow in releasing funds for relief agencies designated to work in the north and had allowed Iraq to assume parts of the distribution programme.

The previous resolution required the United Nations to be in charge of distribution in the north whereas the Baghdad government was to be in charge of supplies in the rest of the country, subject to U.N. monitoring.
